title: What Is AI? 🤖

mascot.name: Chip
mascot.greeting: Hi, I'm Chip! Your phone knows your face. A game knows your next move. How? Let's find out together!

recap: AI learns from lots of examples.
Today's AI is good at one job, not every job.
We can build AI with rules or by letting it learn.

sections.heading: 1. A Computer That Learns
sections.bigIdea: AI is a computer that learns from examples.
sections.chipQuote: Most computers only do what they are told. I can learn!

analogy.description: Your little cousin points at a dog and says "cat". You show her lots of dogs. Soon she gets it right every time.

sections.bodyMarkdown:
A normal computer follows steps, one by one. A step list like this is called an **algorithm**. Type 2 + 2, and it always says 4.

**AI** works in a new way. We show it lots of examples. It looks for what they have in common. Then it can make a good guess about something it has never seen.

jargonBuster.simpleExplanation: A list of steps a computer follows, in order.
Short for artificial intelligence. A computer that learns from examples.

diagram.caption: How AI learns what a dog is
diagram.alt: Four steps: the computer is shown one dog photo, then many more dogs, finds what they share, and then names a dog it has never seen.
steps: We show the computer a photo and say: "This is a dog." 🐶
We show it lots more dogs. Big, small, spotty, fluffy.
It finds what they share: four legs, a wet nose, a waggy tail.
Now it sees a new photo and says: "Dog!" ✅

more.title: Why is it called "artificial"?
more.bodyMarkdown: "Artificial" means made by people. "Intelligence" means being able to learn and solve problems. So AI is learning that people built into a machine.

teen.add: Learning from examples has its own name: **machine learning**. The examples are called data. More good data usually means better guesses.

jargonBuster.simpleExplanation: A way to build AI where the computer finds patterns in data by itself.

checkIn.question: How does AI learn what a dog looks like?
options: 📸 By looking at lots of dog photos
📏 By measuring one dog with a ruler
checkIn.praise: Yes! Lots of examples help AI learn.
checkIn.explanation: AI looks at many examples and finds what they have in common.

sections.heading: 2. Good at One Job
sections.bigIdea: The AI we have today is great at one job.
sections.chipQuote: In films, robots can do everything. Real AI is much more picky!

analogy.description: A toaster makes great toast. Ask it to wash your socks, and nothing happens. It only knows one job.

sections.bodyMarkdown:
The AI in your phone can open it when it sees your face. Another AI picks songs you might like. But the face AI can't pick songs. Each one does just one job.

This is called **narrow AI**. A robot that can learn any job like you can does not exist yet. You only see it in films.

jargonBuster.simpleExplanation: AI that is good at one job and nothing else. All the AI we have today is narrow.

diagram.caption: Real AI today vs film robots
diagram.content:
graph TD
    AI["Kinds of AI"]
    AI --> Narrow["One-job AI: real today 🛠️"]
    AI --> General["Do-anything AI: only in films 🎬"]
    Narrow --> J1["📱 Opens your phone with your face"]
    Narrow --> J2["🎵 Picks songs for you"]
    Narrow --> J3["🗺️ Finds the fastest way home"]
    General --> F1["🤖 Learns any job, like a person (not built yet)"]
diagram.alt: A tree. Kinds of AI split into one-job AI, which is real today and opens phones, picks songs and finds the way home, and do-anything AI, which is only in films and has not been built.

more.title: The do-anything kind
more.bodyMarkdown: Scientists call the do-anything kind "general AI". Some think it will be built one day. Others think it never will. Nobody knows yet.

teen.add: Scientists call the do-anything kind **general AI**. Some chatbots seem to do many jobs. But they still can't learn to ride a bike or cook dinner.

jargonBuster.simpleExplanation: AI that could learn any job a person can. Nobody has built it yet.

checkIn.question: Which one is real AI today?
options: 🤖 A robot that can do every job
🎵 An app that picks songs for you
checkIn.praise: Right! A song picker does one job well.
checkIn.explanation: Today's AI is good at one job, like picking songs.

sections.heading: 3. Person or Computer?
sections.bigIdea: Can you tell a computer from a person just by chatting?
sections.chipQuote: Let's play a game. Can you spot the computer?

analogy.description: You swap notes with two pen pals you can't see. One is a person. One is a computer. Your job is to guess which is which.

sections.bodyMarkdown:
A long time ago, a scientist asked a big question. If you only chat with a computer, can you tell it is not a person? This game is called the **Turing test**.

Some chat apps today sound a lot like people. But sounding like a person is not the same as thinking like one.

jargonBuster.simpleExplanation: A game where you chat and try to tell a computer from a person.

diagram.caption: How the guessing game works
diagram.alt: Four steps: you send the same question to two hidden chat partners, both answer, you read the answers, and you guess which one is the computer.
steps: You send the same question to two hidden pen pals. ✉️
You read both answers. Which one sounds like a person?
You guess which one is the computer. 🕵️

more.title: Who was Turing?
more.bodyMarkdown: Alan Turing was a scientist in England. He came up with this game in 1950, long before phones or chat apps.

teen.add: Many chat apps work by guessing the next word, over and over. They can pass a short chat. But passing the test does not prove that a machine understands what it says.

interactiveWidget.title: 🎮 Game: Spot the Computer
interactiveWidget.instruction: Read both answers. Pick the one you think the computer wrote.

scenario.userPrompt: What did you do last weekend?
scenario.terminalA: Ha, not much! I went to my friend's birthday and ate way too much cake. My tummy hurt after.
scenario.terminalB: Weekend activities commonly include leisure, social gatherings and rest, which support overall well-being.
scenario.explanation: Terminal B sounds like a fact book. It never says what it did. People tell little stories about their own day.

interactiveWidget.goal: Spot the computer, then say how you knew.
interactiveWidget.predictionPrompt: Before you pick: what would a real person say about their weekend?
hints: People talk about things that happened to them.
A computer can sound too neat, like a fact book.
interactiveWidget.successMessage: Great detective work! Telling people from computers is harder than it looks.

sections.heading: 4. Two Ways to Build AI
sections.bigIdea: You can give a computer rules, or let it learn from examples.
sections.chipQuote: How would you teach me to spot a dog?

analogy.metaphorName: The Rule Book and the Photo Album
analogy.description: Way 1 is a rule book. It says: "A dog has four legs and a tail." Way 2 is a photo album full of dogs.

sections.bodyMarkdown:
Way 1: people write the **rules** by hand. Rules work well for clear jobs, like maths. But a dog lying in a box breaks the rules!

Way 2: people give lots of examples. The computer finds the pattern itself. This is how most AI is built today.

jargonBuster.simpleExplanation: Steps that people write by hand, like "if it has a tail, it might be a dog".

diagram.caption: Two ways to build AI
diagram.content:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Way1 ["Way 1: Rules"]
        A1["People write rules 📝"] --> A2["Computer follows them 🔎"] --> A3["Gets stuck on surprises ❌"]
    end
    subgraph Way2 ["Way 2: Learning"]
        B1["People give examples 📸"] --> B2["Computer finds the pattern 🧠"] --> B3["Handles new dogs ✅"]
    end
diagram.alt: Two paths side by side. Way 1: people write rules, the computer follows them, and it gets stuck on surprises. Way 2: people give examples, the computer finds the pattern, and it handles new dogs.

teen.add: Way 1 is called **symbolic AI**. You will meet it in the next lesson. Way 2 is machine learning. Many tools today mix the two.

jargonBuster.simpleExplanation: AI built from rules and facts that people write down.

checkIn.question: A dog is curled up in a box. Which way copes better?
checkIn.praise: Yes! Learning from photos copes with surprises.
checkIn.explanation: Rules break on surprises. Learning from lots of examples copes better.

miniQuiz.question: How does most AI learn?
miniQuiz.praise: Great! Examples are how AI learns.
miniQuiz.explanation: AI looks at lots of examples and finds what they have in common.

miniQuiz.question: Which of these is narrow AI we use today?
options: A robot that can do every job
An app that opens your phone when it sees your face
miniQuiz.praise: Spot on! Face unlock does one job well.
miniQuiz.explanation: Narrow AI is good at one job, like opening your phone with your face.

miniQuiz.question: In the Turing test, what are you trying to guess?
options: Which chat partner is a computer
miniQuiz.praise: Yes! You try to spot the computer.
miniQuiz.explanation: In the Turing test, you chat and try to tell the computer from the person.

miniQuiz.question: What is it called when a computer finds patterns in data by itself?
miniQuiz.praise: Exactly! Machine learning finds the pattern in the data.
miniQuiz.explanation: Machine learning is learning from data. Symbolic AI uses rules people write.

teachBack.prompt: Chip asks: How would you explain AI to a friend?
options: A computer that learns from lots of examples.
A robot that thinks just like a person.
A computer that can do every job.
teachBack.explanation: Right! AI learns from examples. It does not think like a person, and it can't do every job.
